title: Building Agentic Layers
capstone_note: Final lesson of Agentic Horizon and the terminal lesson of the whole 14-lesson arc (TAC 1-8 + AH 1-6). It synthesizes every prior tactic into one buildable object: the agentic layer, graded from Class 1 Grade 1 to Class 3 Grade 3, whose end-state is the codebase singularity.

video.note: recording.json reports a 2880x1620 CDP screen capture at 15fps, but the delivered/encoded MP4 is native 1920x1080 h264. All frames were extracted at native 1920x1080 (no upscaling).

tactic.name: Prioritize Agentics — Build the Agentic Layer
tactic.one_liner: Stop thinking of your codebase as just the application; wrap it in an agentic layer — a graded ring of prompts, sub-agents, skills, closed-loop templates, prompt chains, experts, out-loop AI Developer Workflows, and an orchestrator agent — and keep leveling that layer up until your agents can run the codebase better than you can.
tactic.why_uncomfortable: It asks you to make the machine that builds the product more important than the product, and to keep investing in an asset (the agentic layer) that you must maintain forever, has zero value on a trivial codebase, and only pays off if you push through several 'fall-off' cliffs most engineers quit at (custom tools at Grade 3, closed loops at Grade 4, prompt chains at Grade 6, getting out of the loop at Class 2). Its promised destination — the codebase singularity, where 'nothing ships to production without my teams of agents' and you trust agents to ship more than you trust yourself or your team — sounds, in Dan's own words, 'crazy' and 'far out.' The tactic demands you build toward trusting agents to run production better than you, which is the exact opposite of the control instinct most senior engineers were trained on.
tactic.meta_tactic: This is TACTIC 08 in the on-screen tactic cards: 'Prioritize Agentics — Build the system that builds the system - prioritize your agentic layer.' It is the umbrella tactic under which all of TAC 1-8 and AH 1-6 resolve.

mission: Give you a complete, buildable roadmap for the agentic layer so that, for any codebase (greenfield or existing), you can (1) locate exactly which Class and Grade you are at, (2) name the single missing element that defines the next rung, and (3) build that rung, test it, and feel it move you toward zero-touch engineering and the codebase singularity. The deeper mission closing the whole Agentic Horizon: you are no longer an AI coder — you are an agentic engineer who builds the system that builds the system, a commander of compute whose codebase increasingly runs itself.

codebase_singularity.definition: The moment you, the engineer, realize your agents can now run your codebase better than you can — and you trust them to ship more than you trust yourself or your team, to the point that nothing ships to production without your teams of agents.
codebase_singularity.dan_words: "My agents can now run my codebase better than I can. I trust them to ship more than I trust myself or my team. Nothing ships to production without my teams of agents. Yes, this might sound crazy. It might sound far out."
codebase_singularity.how_you_get_there: You do not start here. You build the agentic layer up Class by Class, Grade by Grade, until the accumulated leverage crosses a threshold. Grade 7 (agent experts) + prompt chaining is where Dan says he first sees agents solving problems end to end without the engineer; Class 3 (orchestrator running AI Developer Workflows) is where it becomes a reliable, observable reality.
codebase_singularity.north_star: Zero-touch engineering (Tactic 7) is the North Star that leads to the codebase singularity; Dan calls it 'not something to fear, it's something to run toward.'
codebase_singularity.misconception: That the codebase singularity is hype about full autonomy arriving tomorrow. Dan frames it as a threshold you build toward incrementally and can attain in a specific, real configuration of a real codebase today — 'there is an agentic layer that could exist inside your codebase, so powerful that your codebase runs itself. The only question now is, do you know how to build it?'

agentic_layer_model.one_liner: Every codebase in the age of agents should now have two layers: an application layer (the code that serves users) and an agentic layer (the ring of agentic primitives that lets agents operate that code on your behalf).
agentic_layer_model.application_layer: The inner, dark squares in Dan's diagram. Bundles EVERYTHING that serves the user: database, frontend, backend, scripts, DevOps, infrastructure, data-science notebooks — and, critically, MULTIPLE applications/repositories, co-located under an apps/ directory (with git submodules if they come from separate repos) so agents can see everything at once.
agentic_layer_model.agentic_layer: The outer, green squares. The new ring where you teach your agents to operate your application on your behalf, as well as and better than you and your team ever could. Made of agentic primitives: prime prompts, memory files, sub-agents, skills, MCP servers, closed-loop prompts, templates, prompt chains, agent experts, out-loop triggers/webhooks, AI Developer Workflows, and an orchestrator agent.
agentic_layer_model.why_bundle_apps: Codebases often contain more than one application. Bundling the agentic layer around ALL related apps lets one team of agents see and operate the whole product surface. Dan's rule: 'You want all of the actual application layer code to run under apps/ and if they're coming from a different git repository I highly recommend you set up git sub modules.'
agentic_layer_model.specialize_dont_genericize: The single most repeated warning in the lesson: do NOT build a generic, one-size-fits-all, reusable agentic layer. Specialize it to fit and wrap ONE codebase for ONE use case. 'Your codebase is literally a specialized solution to solve a problem... build to win for the use cases you care about.'
agentic_layer_model.core_four_recurrence: Everything in the agentic layer — prompt, sub-agent, skill, prompt chain, ADW, orchestrator — eventually reduces to the core four (context, model, prompt, tools). 'It doesn't matter what it's called... everything eventually becomes a core four.' The composite type (skill vs command vs custom agent) does not matter; increasing your compute advantage does.

class_grade_taxonomy.framing: Three concrete CLASSES of agentic layer, each defined by a unique element that distinguishes it from the class below. Within each class, GRADES 1..N measure how powerful your layer is, each grade adding a new dimension. You identify where you are (class + grade), raise your grade, then jump to the next class. Classes are cumulative: every grade and class stacks — Class 3 still contains all of Class 1 and Class 2.

class_jumps.class1_to_class2: In-loop -> Out-loop. You stop sitting in the terminal and let agents run without you (a hard transition).
class_jumps.class2_to_class3: Out-loop -> Orchestrated. You add an orchestrator agent that commands teams of agents (a different type of agentic coding again).

class_1.name: Class 1 — In-loop agentic layer (Layer 1)
class_1.unique_element: Agentic primitives sitting on the first layer, operated by you in the loop.

grades.unique_element: A prime prompt and/or memory files.
grades.plain_english: The thinnest possible agentic layer. A tiny amount of code plus a prime command (an activatable memory file you can fine-tune to run a specific workflow) and/or a CLAUDE.md memory file. If you have this, you technically have an agentic layer.
grades.dan_words: "The thinnest possible agentic layer you can have. A small amount of code and you have a prime prompt and or memory files. It doesn't get thinner than this."
grades.compute_advantage: Clean minimal setup; great foundation for agentic growth; agents understand context immediately; trivially reproducible.
grades.tradeoffs: No value on a codebase this small; useless for large codebases; misses nearly every leverage point of agentic coding.

grades.unique_element: Sub-agents (plus specs/ for plans and ai_docs/ for documentation).
grades.plain_english: Start surrounding the codebase with more leverage: a specs/ directory where plans are written, an ai_docs/ directory agents pull documentation from, and sub-agents you can run (e.g. a fetch-docs sub-agent that saves to ai_docs/, a test-writer). Specialization + the ability to parallelize workflows; plan before you implement.
grades.dan_words: "The big advantages here is that we have specialization with sub-agents and we can scale this and parallelize certain workflows... now we're starting to collect documentation for agents and we're planning our work before we implement."
grades.tradeoffs: Not that novel; many engineers have passed this level; still limited — the big thing missing is custom tools.

grades.unique_element: Custom tools — skills, MCP servers, and prime commands with tool access.
grades.plain_english: Where the agentic layer starts to genuinely wrap the application. All three (skills, MCP servers, prime-with-tools) give the same thing: custom tools that enhance the agent's core four. Crucially, skills and MCP servers can both be replaced by a well-engineered prompt — you can teach an agent to run PSQL/CLI directly (e.g. prime_db) and skip the MCP entirely, since MCPs are token-heavy.
grades.dan_words: "All of these three things give us the same thing, custom tools that enhance our agents core four... Skills and MCP servers can both be replaced with just a simple prompt."
grades.fall_off_warning: A lot of engineers get stuck at Grade 3: they think they got past it but their tools are terrible, don't scale, chew tokens, and are over-engineered. 'One of the most common problems is that engineers will have way too many tools.' Designing tools (via MCP, skills, or raw prompts) is a critical, distinct skill — the subject of the custom-agents lesson (AH-3).
grades.tradeoffs: Prompt and context engineering now become genuinely important; tools must be carefully designed or they burn cash and fail to scale.

grades.plain_english: You start asking your agents to review their own work: request -> validate -> resolve. This is TAC Lesson 5 ('always add feedback loops') embedded into the layer. Self-correcting agents; add more compute to buy more confidence in results. Concrete prompts: review/code-review, reproduce-bug (saves a resolution file into app_review/), test-backend, test-frontend, and fix.
grades.dan_words: "Grade four is distinct in that you start asking your agents to review their work. This is where you realize that you should always add feedback loops into your agentic layer. You're effectively adding more compute to get more confidence in your agent's results... More compute should equal more trust, not less. If it's less, you're doing something wrong."
grades.fall_off_warning: A place engineers fall off and miss out on using more compute to get the job done.
grades.tradeoffs: More complexity; you must know how to prompt-engineer (why AH-2 agentic prompt engineering mattered).

grades.unique_element: Templates — structured plans with specific output formats for different types of work (bug, feature, chore).
grades.plain_english: Where you truly template your engineering and teach your agents to build like YOU do. The way you solve a bug differs from a chore or a new feature, so each gets its own template with a required output format and embedded closed-loop validation. Many engineers write templates without realizing it. Features demand more detail (user story, technical design, back/front/API organization).
grades.codebase_note: In this codebase the bug/feature/chore split is embedded INSIDE plan.md, which classifies task_type (chore|feature|refactor|fix|enhancement) and complexity (simple|medium|complex) and emits conditional sections. The lesson's separate bug.md / feature.md / chore.md / new_api_endpoint.md files are illustrated on-screen as a mock 'example project structure' (frame t1288); the working repo consolidates the idea into the templated plan.md + plan_w_scouters.md.
grades.dan_words: "Templates are structured plans with specific output formats for different types of work. This lets you customize how you want your agent to build. This is where you can truly template your engineering and teach your agents to build like you do."
grades.tradeoffs: You must invest in and maintain them; over-templating can reduce agent flexibility if structures are too strict; templates must evolve as the codebase evolves.

grades.unique_element: Prompt chains / agentic workflows — one prompt references many prompts and/or sub-agents and skills.
grades.plain_english: You stop running single prompts and start chaining them: plan then build; scout then plan. The first versions of the most powerful leverage point of agentic coding — the AI Developer Workflow. Composable, reusable, isolated primitives you can run individually OR chain. Small teams of agents emerge.
grades.dan_words: "When you start chaining together prompts and agents, you are building out the first versions of the most powerful leverage point of agentic coding, the AI developer workflow."
grades.critical_rule: Never build a plan-build-review workflow that cannot ALSO be run as its individual pieces. 'If you slam this onto one and you can't run the individual pieces, at some point something will go wrong and you will not be able to isolate the one thing that went wrong.' This also makes it easy to scale pieces into parallel sub-agents.
grades.hard_requirement: Context engineering (the R&D framework, AH-1) becomes a REQUIREMENT here: 'You can't write a five agent long prompt chain without knowing the context that every agent will have at every step.' You must adopt your agent's perspective.
grades.tradeoffs: You must know what you want to build; chains are harder to debug, especially near the context-window limit.

grades.unique_element: Agent experts — agents that keep a domain-specific mental model of an area of your codebase.
grades.plain_english: Deploy experts into your codebase (AH-5). An expert keeps an expertise.yaml mental model (NOT a source of truth — the code is), knows file references, and has surrounding specialized prompts (question, plan, build) that can be chained. This is where Dan says he first sees agents solving problems end to end without you — the doorstep of the codebase singularity via zero-touch (Tactic 7).
grades.act_learn_reuse: Each expert implements ACT -> LEARN -> REUSE: question.md (REUSE: read expertise.yaml, validate against code, answer with file/line citations), plan.md (ACT: expertise-informed planning), self-improve.md (LEARN: diff expertise.yaml against the real code, remedy discrepancies, enforce a MAX_LINES cap, validate YAML), plan_build_improve.md (the full loop).
grades.dan_words: "Class one, grade seven is uniquely identified by agent experts... The question for you is, do you have a specialized agent that can operate specific parts of your codebase better than you can, increasingly so."
grades.form_factor_note: The composite type does not matter — an expert can be a set of prompts (Dan's recommended default), a custom sub-agent, a skill, or a prime prompt. Everything turns into context/model/prompt/tools.
grades.tradeoffs: Requires a high level of prompt engineering and context engineering; YOU have to be the expert in the domain you build agents for.

class_2.name: Class 2 — Out-loop agentic layer (Layer 2)
class_2.unique_element: An out-loop system: agents that operate your codebase without you sitting in the terminal. Introduced in TAC Lesson 4 (AFK Agents); called the 'PITER framework' on-screen (auto-transcribed 'Peter framework').

grades.unique_element: The out-loop fabric — a webhook / external trigger that fires prompts against your codebase through a core agent SDK. Fabric only, no full ADW yet.
grades.plain_english: Expose an HTTP endpoint (with security) so an external service — Slack, Jira, Discord, GitHub — can execute prompts against your codebase from out of the loop. The webhook calls your prompt, which runs against a core Agent SDK that fires a slew of custom agents (planner, builder). This is where programmatic/custom agents (AH-3, the Claude Agent SDK) become critical, and where the deterministic scripting layer for orchestrating agents begins.
grades.codebase_note: The lesson's slide shows adw_trigger/adw_webhook.py + adw_modules/adw_agent_core.py + adw_modules/prompt.py. In the working repo the out-loop entry points are (a) the orchestrator's start_adw MCP tool and (b) the CLI adw_manual_trigger.py; both create an ai_developer_workflows DB record then spawn a detached background process via adw_scripts.py (subprocess.Popen(['uv','run', workflow_path, '--adw-id', adw_id], start_new_session=True)). A literal inbound GitHub/Slack webhook is described conceptually; the repo implements the DB-record + background-spawn fabric it would call.
grades.dan_words: "Class two, also known as layer two, is where you build out an out loop system... you can just execute prompts against your code base from an external service, right, from out the loop... This is Outloop agentic coding. This is where we start building up a deterministic scripting layer for orchestrating our agents."

grades.unique_element: Full AI Developer Workflows (ADWs) — deterministic code orchestrating non-deterministic agents, end to end.
grades.plain_english: The highest leverage point of agentic coding. Deterministic Python controls step order, file paths, logging, validation, retries, and DB writes; non-deterministic Claude agents do the reasoning and code generation. You get full control BETWEEN each agent step and can emit progress to a UI (Dan uses WebSockets; TAC used GitHub issue/PR comments). Your prompt chains disappear and get replaced by concrete ADWs with great logging and observability.
grades.dan_words: "class two, grade two is huge because we now have AI developer workflows. As mentioned, this is the highest leverage point of Agentic Coding. Why is that? It's because you get deterministic code plus non-deterministic agents. You get the best of both worlds. You get full control in between each agent step, right? We're talking logging, validation, retries."
grades.vs_cloud_tools: Dan's contrast: many engineers will just adopt an out-loop cloud agentic-coding tool from a big lab and stop. Fine — but they won't get the control advantage of building your OWN ADWs, which is how you keep the highest control over your most important asset: your codebase.
grades.tradeoffs: You have to write and maintain all of it; nothing is free in engineering.

class_3.name: Class 3 — Orchestrated agentic layer
class_3.unique_element: The orchestrator agent — 'the one agent to rule them all.' A custom lead-engineer agent that runs CRUD on other agents.

grades.unique_element: The orchestrator agent itself — a custom agent that CRUDs, commands, and manages other agents.
grades.plain_english: A custom lead-engineer agent placed in its own application or inside the ADWs directory. It gives centralized control over your whole agentic layer and can also serve as your out-loop system. It can be in the terminal (in the loop) OR out-loop; the best version is out-loop and fine-tuned. You reuse sub-agents as command-level agents (fixer, reviewer, builder) and expose orchestrator tools. This is AH-4 (Multi-Agent Orchestration, the O-agent).
grades.dan_words: "This is the orchestrator agent, the one agent to rule them all... what you're effectively doing here is building a custom agent that is a lead engineer that can CRUD command and manage other agents... This gives you centralized control over your agentic layer."
grades.pipeline: The orchestrator is the top of the agent pipeline every engineer walks: base agent -> better agent -> more agents -> custom agents -> orchestrator agent.
grades.tradeoffs: Hard to build; requires experience and skill above the pack; hard to maintain (orchestrating an orchestrator that runs other agents). But 'the impact here is absurd.'

grades.unique_element: Orchestrator Developer Workflows — the orchestrator conducts multi-agent, multi-team workflows via slash commands.
grades.plain_english: Feels like a prompt chain or ADW, but the orchestrator (which understands your agents, prompts, and skills) prompts and communicates back-and-forth with command-level agents, spinning up multiple teams focused on multiple problems. A multi-level conversation; you can talk to any agent in the workflow at any time and keep pushing. Full observability: every event summarized by a summary agent and reported back. One agent, one prompt, one purpose (Tactic 6) at scale.
grades.dan_words: "once you have built your orchestrator... you can now build out orchestrator developer workflows... now you're prompting a orchestrator that understands your agents, your prompts, your skills that then prompts and communicates back and forth with your command level agents... your orchestrator agent can spin up multiple teams of agents focused on multiple problems."
grades.caveat: These rely on non-deterministic systems for large, massive chains. Powerful, but the orchestrator 'fires this off and walks away' — which motivates Grade 3.

grades.unique_element: The orchestrator running AI Developer Workflows (raw-code ADWs) — the final level.
grades.plain_english: Give the orchestrator the ability to run AI Developer Workflows (which use raw deterministic code) so its biggest jobs become trackable, observable, controllable, and reliably validated instead of relying purely on non-deterministic chains. The final UI has BOTH the log-stream view and the ADW's (swimlane) view, showing full end-to-end pipelines. This is Dan's 'final gift' codebase (orchestrator-agent-with-adws) and the knock on the door of the codebase singularity.
grades.dan_words: "The last piece to our class three, grade three system is this... AI developer workflow plan build. The big difference between our orchestrator developer workflows is that this can use raw code... by giving our orchestrator the ability to run AI developer workflows. We now reach the final stage... We now have both the log stream view and we have the ADW's view."
grades.high_trust_source: The big piece where you can have HIGH trust in the system is the AI Developer Workflow (deterministic code orchestrating non-deterministic agents), because it is observable and controllable.

class_grade_taxonomy.goal_reminder: The goal is NOT to sprint to the highest class. It is to (1) recognize where you are, (2) name the pieces you have and the pieces you are missing (many engineers are missing agent experts), and (3) make a plan to build the missing rungs, test them, and see how they progress you. Every class grants a new capability.

core_concepts.name: The Agentic Layer (the new ring around your codebase)
core_concepts.plain_english: The single most important mental framework of the entire course: a new ring around your application layer where you teach agents to operate your codebase on your behalf, as well as and better than you and your team ever could. Building it is the highest-ROI action for any engineer in the age of agents.
core_concepts.dan_words: "There is one mental framework that sits at the center, an idea so important that if you capture it, it can change the way you engineer forever. The agentic layer. This is the new ring around your codebase where you teach your agents to operate your application on your behalf as well and even better than you and your team ever could."
core_concepts.misconception: That the agentic layer is 'just my .claude folder' or 'just prompts.' It is a graded, specialized system (prompts -> experts -> ADWs -> orchestrator) that wraps ALL your related applications and that you invest in and maintain like a first-class product.

core_concepts.name: The Codebase Singularity
core_concepts.plain_english: The threshold moment when your agents can run your codebase better than you can and you trust them to ship more than you trust yourself or your team. The North Star destination of both TAC and AH.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Once you've built a sufficiently powerful agentic layer, something will happen. The codebase singularity... My agents can now run my codebase better than I can."
core_concepts.misconception: Reading it as fear/job-loss. Dan: 'This is not something to fear, it's something to run toward.' It is an asymmetric advantage available to engineers who build the layer.

core_concepts.name: The Class/Grade system (a maturity model for your agentic layer)
core_concepts.plain_english: A ruler for your agentic layer. Three classes (in-loop, out-loop, orchestrated) each defined by a unique element; grades 1..N within each class each add a dimension. You locate yourself, raise your grade, then jump classes. Everything stacks — Class 3 still contains Class 1 and Class 2.
core_concepts.dan_words: "There are three concrete classes of the agentic layer. Class one, class two, and class three, each defined by a unique element that makes them distinct from the rest... Every class is going to have one to N grades that will give you a rough understanding of how powerful your agentic layer is."
core_concepts.misconception: That you must be at Class 3 to be doing it right. The point is self-location and next-step planning, not maxing the class. A specialized Class 1 Grade 5 layer can outperform a generic Class 3 one.

core_concepts.name: Application layer vs Agentic layer (and bundling apps)
core_concepts.plain_english: Two layers per codebase: application (all the code that serves users, including MULTIPLE apps under apps/) and agentic (the ring of primitives that operate it). Co-locate related repos (git submodules) so agents see everything at once.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The green squares here, the outer layer, this is the new agentic layer. The inner layer here, these dark squares, this is going to be your application layer. And we're bundling a ton of things underneath your application layer... so that we can bundle your different repositories underneath your agentic layer."
core_concepts.misconception: That each app needs its own agentic layer. If your agent needs to see multiple related codebases, bundle them under one specialized agentic layer; if not, it is fine to duplicate and specialize a separate layer per codebase. Specialize either way.

core_concepts.name: Specialize your agentic layer (do not build for reuse)
core_concepts.plain_english: The most repeated warning: do not build a generic, reusable, one-size-fits-all agentic layer. Shape every prompt, template, and agent to ONE codebase and ONE use case. Specialization is how you build a distinguished, unique product through both layers.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Engineers go wrong here too. They think they need to build a generic one size fits all agentic layer. That is not what we're doing here at all. Your agentic layer should be specialized to fit and wrap your codebase... Don't focus on reuse... Focus on making these prompts great, for that one codebase."
core_concepts.misconception: That reuse/DRY is the goal. Here, specialization is the goal; templates and experts are deliberately tuned to your codebase's exact problems.

core_concepts.name: AI Developer Workflow (ADW) — the highest leverage point
core_concepts.plain_english: Deterministic code orchestrating non-deterministic agents. Raw agents are unreliable; raw code is inflexible; combined they are unstoppable. Deterministic Python owns step order, file paths, logging, validation, retries, DB writes; agents own reasoning and code generation. Full control between each step, plus observability.
core_concepts.dan_words: "you get deterministic code plus non-deterministic agents. You get the best of both worlds. You get full control in between each agent step... logging, validation, retries."
core_concepts.codebase_grounding: adws/adw_workflows/adw_plan_build.py sets TOTAL_STEPS = 2 and runs run_plan_step (invokes /plan via the Skill tool) then run_build_step (/build), with create_logging_hooks + create_message_handlers logging every TextBlock/ThinkingBlock/ToolUseBlock and StepStart/StepEnd to the DB and broadcasting over WebSocket to the swimlane UI.
core_concepts.misconception: That an ADW is just a prompt chain. A prompt chain is agent-driven and non-deterministic end to end; an ADW wraps agent steps in deterministic code so you can validate, retry, log, and observe each transition. Dan: your prompt chains 'start disappearing and they turn into AI developer workflows.'

core_concepts.name: The Orchestrator Agent (one agent to rule them all)
core_concepts.plain_english: A custom lead-engineer agent that runs CRUD on other agents and can also kick off AI Developer Workflows. Centralized control over the whole agentic layer; usually the out-loop system too. The top of the base -> better -> more -> custom -> orchestrator pipeline.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is the orchestrator agent, the one agent to rule them all... a custom agent that is a lead engineer that can CRUD command and manage other agents."
core_concepts.codebase_grounding: The real orchestrator (apps/orchestrator_3_stream) is a Claude Agent SDK agent (default model claude-opus-4-5-20251101) whose system prompt (orchestrator_agent_system_prompt.md, 'You are the conductor of this multi-agent orchestra') exposes 10 MCP tools via create_management_tools(): 8 agent-management tools (create_agent, list_agents, command_agent, check_agent_status, delete_agent, interrupt_agent, read_system_logs, report_cost) PLUS start_adw and check_adw — the exact bridge that lets Class 3 run Class 2's ADWs.
core_concepts.misconception: That the orchestrator kicks off ADWs by the user typing a magic 'start adw:' chat string. In the real code there is no literal 'start adw:' parser — the orchestrator LLM emits a start_adw MCP tool call, which writes a DB record and spawns a detached uv-run workflow process.

core_concepts.name: Zero-touch engineering & the meta-tactic 'Prioritize Agentics'
core_concepts.plain_english: Zero-touch engineering (Tactic 7): one-shot, end-to-end, prompt-to-production workflows that run with no human touch. The meta-tactic (Tactic 8) that contains everything: prioritize agentics — build the system that builds the system, prioritize your agentic layer, because it is the highest-leverage activity for any engineer now.
core_concepts.dan_words: "all of this can be boiled down into one meta tactic, right? Prioritize agentics. Build the system that builds the system. Prioritize your agentic layer... You're building the machine that builds your product now."
core_concepts.misconception: That zero-touch is a distant meme. Dan: 'This is not a dream anymore. It's not a meme or a distant thing in the future. This is what some engineers are doing right now.'

recap_of_the_whole_course.framing: The lesson closes by boiling TAC + AH into the tactics that build the agentic layer, then recapping the AH arc.

tactics_restated.name: Stop coding
tactics_restated.restatement: Use the best tool for the job, agents. If you still write code by hand you will not reach any sufficiently complex agentic layer.

tactics_restated.name: Adopt your agent's perspective
tactics_restated.restatement: Think as your agents would; give them the leverage points they need to ship. Before you hit enter, ask: could YOU solve this with exactly this context? Critical for building teams of agents. (AH-1 R&D / context engineering.)

tactics_restated.name: Template your engineering
tactics_restated.restatement: Encode what you would do into prompts/plans/templates ('this is how we solve bugs, build API endpoints, integrate this service'). Non-deterministic models drift; templates are your roadmap to repeated success.

tactics_restated.name: Stay out the loop
tactics_restated.restatement: Scale agentic workflows/prompt chains, then get out of the terminal. This forces you to build the system that builds the system; you will not scale stuck prompting back and forth.

tactics_restated.name: Always add feedback loops
tactics_restated.restatement: Closed-loop prompts (request, validate, resolve) so agents validate their own work. More compute should equal more trust, not less.

tactics_restated.name: One agent, one prompt, one purpose (let your agents focus)
tactics_restated.restatement: A focused agent is a performant agent. Two tasks in one prompt lowers the odds of both. With the orchestrator you spin agents up when needed and delete them when done. Don't fight the context, use it.

tactics_restated.name: Target zero-touch engineering
tactics_restated.restatement: One-shot prompt-to-production workflows; the doorstep of the codebase singularity. Do it via context + prompt engineering.

tactics_restated.name: Prioritize agentics (meta-tactic)
tactics_restated.restatement: Build the system that builds the system; prioritize your agentic layer. The umbrella over all the others.

ah_arc_restated.name: Elite context engineering (R&D framework)
ah_arc_restated.point: None of the tactics matter if you can't prompt and manage your agents' context windows. Manage context with the R&D framework; this is where one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose comes in.

ah_arc_restated.name: Agentic prompt engineering (seven levels of prompt formats)
ah_arc_restated.point: The first AH lesson; powerful prompt engineering underlies every template and chain.

ah_arc_restated.name: Building custom agents
ah_arc_restated.point: To build programmatic agents you must learn to build custom agents (this lesson deployed eight). This is how you build the orchestrator.

ah_arc_restated.name: Multi-agent orchestration (the O-agent)
ah_arc_restated.point: The next paradigm: terminal -> out of terminal (external service) -> a manager of your agents you run against. Multi-agent is the future.

ah_arc_restated.name: Agent experts
ah_arc_restated.point: The most slept-on, highest-ROI opportunity. Build experts into custom agents, programmatically, with customized system prompt/tools/user prompts to solve one problem extraordinarily well. The future of product and codebases with agents.

ah_arc_restated.name: Building agentic layers (this lesson)
ah_arc_restated.point: Assemble it all into the graded agentic layer and attain the codebase singularity.

recap_of_the_whole_course.dans_next_move: Dan's stated next-year plan: build a valuable four-to-five-figure-per-month business using every TAC/AH tactic and record the entire process end to end, to prove what a single engineer can do; possibly rolled into a future course if successful. If it fails he will not put out another product on his own for some time.

step_by_step_demo: (00:36-05:48) Framing: everything built toward one moment — the codebase singularity. Dan introduces the agentic layer as the central framework and the highest-ROI action, defines the singularity ('my agents can now run my codebase better than I can'), and previews three classes and their grades.

(05:48-06:45) The core diagram (frame t0382): green outer squares = agentic layer, dark inner squares = application layer; Class 1/2/3 shown as progressively larger rings, each with Grade 1...N. Application layer bundles DB, front/back end, scripts, DevOps, notebooks, and multiple apps.

(07:36-09:36) Destination demo (frame t0558): Dan jumps straight to a Class-3 out-loop orchestrator system. He opens the prompt interface, notes a new 'highest leverage point' section — the orchestrator can now kick off AI Developer Workflows — and fires two workflows (plan_build_review_fix for a markdown-preview app, and a simple plan_build). The UI shows the LOGS view and the ADW's (swimlane) view, two workflows running end to end; 'the orchestrator doesn't need to do anything, this runs end to end.'
(09:36-10:35) Reset to zero: 'we don't start at class three... we start with nothing.' Every codebase should now have two components — application layer and agentic layer.

(10:35-13:00) Class 1 Grade 1: the thinnest layer — a prime command + CLAUDE.md memory. Dan opens an example project structure showing .claude/commands/prime and CLAUDE.md. Compute advantage: clean, minimal, instantly understood; tradeoff: no value at this size.

(13:00-14:30) Class 1 Grade 2 (frame t0812): add specs/ (plans), ai_docs/ (docs), and sub-agents (a fetch-docs sub-agent on Haiku saving to ai_docs/, a test-writer). Specialization + parallelization; plan before implement.

(14:30-17:20) Class 1 Grade 3 (frame t0895): custom tools — .mcp.json (postgres, firecrawl, atlassian/JIRA, notion), skills (start/stop app via a script; no MCP needed), and prime-with-tools (prime_db teaching PSQL). Warning: many engineers get stuck here with too many bad tools that burn tokens.

(17:20-20:40) Class 1 Grade 4 (frame t1088): closed-loop prompts — review/code-review, reproduce-bug (writes to app_review/), test-backend/test-frontend, fix. Request -> validate -> resolve. More compute = more trust.

(20:40-25:50) Class 1 Grade 5 (frame t1288): templates — bug.md, feature.md, chore.md, new_api_endpoint.md, etc. Teach agents to build like you; embed closed-loop validation in each template. Warning against over-templating. Dan also lays out the winning multi-app structure: everything under apps/ with git submodules for related repos.

(25:50-30:36) Class 1 Grade 6 (frame t1768): prompt chains / agentic workflows — plan-then-build, scout-then-plan (scout_then_plan.md launches parallel scouts via the Task tool, then plans). The first versions of the ADW. Rule: always be able to run the pieces individually. Context engineering becomes a hard requirement.

(30:36-35:48) Class 1 Grade 7 (frame t2015): agent experts — .claude/commands/experts/<domain>/ with expertise.yaml (mental model), question/plan/self-improve/plan_build_improve prompts (ACT/LEARN/REUSE). Where agents start solving problems end to end without you; doorstep of the singularity.

(35:48-40:00) Class 2 Grade 1 (frame t2258): out-loop fabric — a webhook/HTTP endpoint (from Slack/Jira/Discord/GitHub) that fires prompts through a core Agent SDK firing custom agents (planner, builder). The deterministic scripting layer begins. No full ADW yet.

(40:00-44:00) Class 2 Grade 2 (frame t2464): full AI Developer Workflows — the outer ring now labeled with adw_plan_build.py, adw_chore_test_merge.py, adw_plan_w_scouts.py, etc. Deterministic code + non-deterministic agents; full control between steps; prompt chains get replaced by concrete ADWs. The highest leverage point.

(44:00-48:30) Class 3 Grade 1: the orchestrator agent — 'one agent to rule them all.' Placed in its own app or in the ADWs directory. Reuses command-level agents (fixer, reviewer, builder) and exposes orchestrator tools. CRUD on agents; centralized control; usually the out-loop system.

(48:30-51:00) Class 3 Grade 2: orchestrator developer workflows — the orchestrator conducts multi-team, multi-agent workflows via .claude/commands (orch_one_shot_agent, orch_scout_and_build, orch_plan_w_scouts_build_review). Multi-level conversation; every event summarized; you can talk to any agent mid-workflow.

(51:00-52:30) Class 3 Grade 3 (frames t2776, t3124): the final level — the orchestrator runs AI Developer Workflows (raw code) for trust/observability. Dan reveals the final UI with both the log-stream view and the ADW's view, calling the orchestrator-agent-with-adws codebase 'my final gift to you here in Agentic Horizon.'

(52:30-55:00) Zoom out: the goal is to locate your class/grade and build the missing pieces, not to sprint to Class 3. Each class grants a new capability; the class jumps (in-loop -> out-loop -> orchestrated) are the hard, meaningful transitions.

(55:00-59:00) Recap of the tactics (stop coding; adopt the agent's perspective; template your engineering; stay out the loop; feedback loops; one agent one prompt one purpose; target zero-touch) culminating in Tactic 08 'Prioritize Agentics' (frame t3518).

(59:00-66:24) AH arc recap (context engineering -> agentic prompt engineering -> custom agents -> multi-agent orchestration -> agent experts), gratitude, the closing idea ('we started orchestrating intelligence'), and Dan's next-year plan to build an agent-run business on camera.

quotes.text: There is one mental framework that sits at the center, an idea so important that if you capture it, it can change the way you engineer forever. The agentic layer.
This is the new ring around your codebase where you teach your agents to operate your application on your behalf as well and even better than you and your team ever could.
Focusing on building the agentic layer of your codebase is the highest return on investment action for any engineer in the age of agents.
My agents can now run my codebase better than I can. I trust them to ship more than I trust myself or my team. Nothing ships to production without my teams of agents.
There is an agentic layer that could exist inside your codebase, so powerful that your codebase runs itself. The only question now is, do you know how to build it?
The green squares here, the outer layer, this is the new agentic layer. The inner layer here, these dark squares, this is going to be your application layer.
Our orchestrator agent can now kick off AI developer workflows.
This is what the future of engineering looks like, fine-tuned to your specific domain, to your specific use case.
The thinnest possible agentic layer you can have. A small amount of code and you have a prime prompt and or memory files.
All of these three things give us the same thing, custom tools that enhance our agents core four.
Skills and MCP servers can both be replaced with just a simple prompt.
You should always add feedback loops into your agentic layer. You're effectively adding more compute to get more confidence in your agent's results.
This is where you can truly template your engineering and teach your agents to build like you do.
Your agentic layer should be specialized to fit and wrap your codebase.
When you start chaining together prompts and agents, you are building out the first versions of the most powerful leverage point of agentic coding, the AI developer workflow.
I would absolutely never build a plan, build, review workflow that cannot be run individually.
Everything is just a context model and prompt. It doesn't matter what it's called... everything eventually becomes a core four.
Class one, grade seven is uniquely identified by agent experts.
This is Outloop agentic coding. This is where we start building up a deterministic scripting layer for orchestrating our agents.
You get deterministic code plus non-deterministic agents. You get the best of both worlds. You get full control in between each agent step.
This is the orchestrator agent, the one agent to rule them all.
What you're effectively doing here is building a custom agent that is a lead engineer that can CRUD command and manage other agents. This gives you centralized control over your agentic layer.
This is my final gift to you here in Agentic Horizon.
We now have both the log stream view and we have the ADW's view.
This is the North Star of TAC. This is the North Star of Agentic Horizon. You wanna push your agents to engineer like you can and better than you can.
More compute should equal more trust, not less. If it's less, you're doing something wrong. Request, validate, resolve.
One agent, one prompt, one purpose. Don't fight the context, use it to your advantage. Let your agents focus.

Target zero-touch engineering, because when you do this, you move closer toward that code-based singularity, the moment when your agents can ship better than you and your team. This is not something to fear, it's something to run toward.
Prioritize agentics. Build the system that builds the system. Prioritize your agentic layer.
When the agents arrived, something changed. We weren't just AI Coding anymore. We started orchestrating intelligence.
If you take the ideas from TAC and AH and apply them, really put them to work... If you do this right, it will change everything.

prerequisites_tools: Everything from TAC 1-8 and AH 1-5 (this is the capstone): agentic prompts, the core four, sub-agents, skills, closed loops, templates, the R&D/context framework, custom agents (Claude Agent SDK), multi-agent orchestration, and agent experts
Claude Code + a Claude plan or Anthropic API funds (millions of tokens across the course)
Terminal, Git (and git submodules for multi-repo bundling), an IDE (Dan uses VS Code)
Python 3.12+ with Astral UV; Node.js 18+ with Bun (for the orchestrator frontend)
PostgreSQL (NeonDB free tier recommended) for the orchestrator/ADW database
Anthropic API key; optional MCP servers seen in .mcp.json.sample (playwright, neon, firecrawl)
what_student_must_internalize: Every codebase now has two layers — application and agentic — and building/leveling the agentic layer is the highest-ROI action available to an engineer.
The agentic layer is measurable: locate your Class (in-loop / out-loop / orchestrated) and Grade, then build the ONE element that defines the next rung. Everything stacks.
The seven Class-1 grades are a concrete build order: prime+memory -> sub-agents -> custom tools -> closed loops -> templates -> prompt chains -> experts.
The two class jumps are the hard, valuable transitions: get OUT of the loop (Class 2), then add an ORCHESTRATOR (Class 3).
The AI Developer Workflow (deterministic code + non-deterministic agents) is the highest leverage point — it is how you keep control and observability while agents do the work.
The orchestrator agent is a custom lead engineer that CRUDs other agents AND can fire ADWs (the class-3-runs-class-2 bridge); it is the top of base->better->more->custom->orchestrator.
Specialize, do not genericize. Build the layer to win for one codebase and one use case; do not chase reuse.
Everything reduces to the core four; the composite form (skill vs command vs custom agent) does not matter — increasing compute advantage does.
The destination is the codebase singularity via zero-touch engineering — something to run toward, attainable in a real configuration of a real codebase today.
The meta-tactic that contains all the others: prioritize agentics — build the system that builds the system.
common_weak_student_failures: Trying to sprint straight to Class 3 (orchestrator) without building Class 1 grades, then drowning in an unmaintainable, non-deterministic mess. Dan: 'we don't start at class three.'
Getting stuck at Grade 3 with too many bad, token-heavy, over-engineered tools and believing they've moved past it — instead of learning to give agents only the tools they need.
Skipping Grade 4 feedback loops (or reading 'more compute' as waste) and never letting agents self-correct — the exact place engineers fall off.
Confusing a plan and a template (Grade 5) and building ad-hoc prompts forever, so agents never learn to build like you and drift on every run.
Building one giant plan-build-review chain that can't be run piece-by-piece (Grade 6), so when it fails you can't isolate the broken step.
Writing multi-agent prompt chains without adopting the agent's perspective / context engineering — required from Grade 6 on, non-negotiable at Grade 7.
Building a generic, reusable, one-size-fits-all agentic layer instead of a specialized one — the single most-warned-against mistake.
Refusing to get out of the loop (Class 1 -> Class 2), staying stuck prompting back-and-forth in the terminal, so the layer never scales.
Treating expertise.yaml as a source of truth instead of a mental model the agent validates against the code (the code is the source of truth).
Believing the codebase singularity is hype/fear rather than a threshold you build toward — and therefore never setting it as the target.
teach_back_prompt: Without notes, teach a colleague the agentic layer. (1) Draw the two layers (application vs agentic) and explain why you bundle multiple apps under one specialized agentic layer. (2) Walk the Class-1 ladder Grade 1->7, naming the unique element each grade adds and giving one real file from the orchestrator-agent-with-adws repo per grade. (3) Explain the two class jumps: what changes going in-loop -> out-loop (Class 2) and out-loop -> orchestrated (Class 3). (4) Define an AI Developer Workflow and why 'deterministic code + non-deterministic agents' is the highest leverage point, using adw_plan_build.py's plan->build steps as evidence. (5) Explain how a Class-3 orchestrator can run a Class-2 ADW (name the exact tool). Finish by defining the codebase singularity and resolving Dan's paradox: why is building the machine that could replace your hands the way you become irreplaceable?

retrieval_questions.q: What are the two layers every codebase should now have, and which squares represent which in Dan's diagram?
retrieval_questions.a: The application layer (inner dark squares — DB, front/back end, scripts, DevOps, notebooks, and multiple bundled apps) and the agentic layer (outer green squares — the ring of primitives that lets agents operate the app on your behalf).

retrieval_questions.q: Name the three classes and the unique element that defines each.
retrieval_questions.a: Class 1 = in-loop agentic primitives; Class 2 = an out-loop system (webhooks/triggers, agents run without you); Class 3 = an orchestrator agent that CRUDs other agents. Everything stacks.

retrieval_questions.q: List the seven Class-1 grades in order.
retrieval_questions.a: 1 prime prompt + memory files; 2 sub-agents (+ specs/, ai_docs/); 3 custom tools (skills, MCP servers, prime-with-tools); 4 closed-loop prompts; 5 templates (bug/feature/chore); 6 prompt chains / agentic workflows; 7 agent experts.

retrieval_questions.q: What defines Class 2 Grade 1 vs Class 2 Grade 2?
retrieval_questions.a: Grade 1 is the out-loop fabric only (a webhook/trigger firing prompts through a core Agent SDK — no full ADW yet); Grade 2 adds the full AI Developer Workflows (deterministic code orchestrating non-deterministic agents).

retrieval_questions.q: Why is the AI Developer Workflow called the highest leverage point of agentic coding?
retrieval_questions.a: Because you get deterministic code PLUS non-deterministic agents — the best of both worlds: full control between each agent step (logging, validation, retries, observability) with the creative capability of frontier agents.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the exact mechanism by which a Class-3 orchestrator runs a Class-2 ADW?
retrieval_questions.a: The orchestrator LLM calls its start_adw MCP tool (one of its 10 tools). That writes an ai_developer_workflows record to Postgres and spawns a detached background process (uv run adws/adw_workflows/adw_<type>.py --adw-id <uuid>) via adw_scripts.py; progress is tracked with check_adw and streamed to the swimlane UI over WebSocket.

The moment you realize your agents can run your codebase better than you can, and you trust them to ship more than you trust yourself or your team — to the point nothing ships to production without your teams of agents.

retrieval_questions.q: What is Dan's single most repeated warning about how to build the agentic layer?
retrieval_questions.a: Specialize it, do not genericize it. Build to win for ONE codebase and ONE use case; do not chase reuse or a one-size-fits-all layer.

retrieval_questions.q: Why must every step of a plan-build-review chain also be runnable individually?
retrieval_questions.a: So that when something goes wrong you can isolate the one broken step, and so each piece can be scaled into parallel sub-agents. If you fuse it into one un-decomposable run you lose both.

retrieval_questions.q: What is an expertise.yaml, and is it a source of truth?
retrieval_questions.a: It's an agent expert's mental model / working memory of a codebase domain. It is NOT a source of truth — the code is; the expert validates the expertise file against the code (via self-improve, the LEARN step) and reuses it to answer/plan.

retrieval_questions.q: What is Tactic 08, the meta-tactic that contains the rest?
retrieval_questions.a: Prioritize agentics — build the system that builds the system, prioritize your agentic layer.

retrieval_questions.q: Which model powers the real orchestrator, and what are its two ADW-specific tools?
retrieval_questions.a: By default claude-opus-4-5-20251101 (config.ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL). Its two ADW tools are start_adw and check_adw (on top of the 8 agent-management tools).

layer_mapping.class_1_in_loop: .claude/ (24 commands, 7 sub-agents, 2 skills, 3 experts, 9 hooks, 11 output-styles, 1 status line) + specs/ + ai_docs/ + app_review/ + app_fix_reports/

grade1_prime_memory..claude/commands/prime.md: Prime prompt: runs git ls-files, reads README + orchestrator core files, summarizes understanding. Focus: apps/orchestrator_3_stream/*.
grade1_prime_memory..claude/commands/prime_cc.md: 'Prime Claude Code': runs prime.md then reads the whole .claude/ tree to focus on the agentic layer itself.
grade1_prime_memory..claude/commands/prime_nile.md: Primes the Nile adaptive-shopping app (model: opus); documents the Agent Expert / ACT->LEARN->REUSE pattern.
grade1_prime_memory.CLAUDE.md: Root memory file: engineering rules (no-mock tests, keep models.py in sync with migrations, use UV never raw python, prefer pydantic, don't commit unless asked, actually read the whole file).

grade2_subagents_specs_docs..claude/agents/build-agent.md: opus. Implements ONE file to a detailed spec in parallel build workflows.
grade2_subagents_specs_docs..claude/agents/docs-scraper.md: sonnet. Scrapes a URL (firecrawl->WebFetch) and saves verbatim markdown to ai_docs/. (On-screen the lesson calls it a 'fetch docs' sub-agent on Haiku — see frame t0812.)
grade2_subagents_specs_docs..claude/agents/planner.md: opus. Lightweight wrapper delegating to the /plan slash command.
grade2_subagents_specs_docs..claude/agents/scout-report-suggest.md: opus. Read-only codebase scout (Read/Glob/Grep); never edits.
grade2_subagents_specs_docs..claude/agents/scout-report-suggest-fast: haiku. Byte-identical body to scout-report-suggest but on the fast/cheap model — the swarm scout.
grade2_subagents_specs_docs..claude/agents/playwright-validator.md: opus. Browser-automation validator via Playwright MCP.
grade2_subagents_specs_docs.ai_docs/: Cached scraped docs for agent context; ai_docs/README.md holds the source-URL list refreshed by /load_ai_docs + docs-scraper.

Boots the Orchestrator 3 Stream backend (start_be.sh) + frontend (start_fe.sh) and opens Chrome; supports --session/--cwd. How Dan launches the orchestrator.
grade3_custom_tools..claude/skills/meta-skill/SKILL.md: 'creating-new-skills' — the skill that writes skills (progressive disclosure, gerund naming, <500 lines) + 3 reference docs.
grade3_custom_tools..mcp.json.sample: MCP server config: playwright, neon, firecrawl-mcp. (Lesson slide also shows postgres/atlassian/notion — see frame t0895.)
grade3_custom_tools.apps/orchestrator_3_stream/.claude/skill: Skill generating new sub-agent config files (has templates/subagent-template.md).

grade4_closed_loops..claude/commands/review.md: model: opus, ANALYSIS-ONLY. Analyzes git diffs, categorizes issues into 4 risk tiers (Blocker/High/Medium/Low), ends with PASS/FAIL; writes app_review/review_<timestamp>.md. Contains a full structured report template.
grade4_closed_loops..claude/commands/fix.md: model: opus, BUILDS. Reads a review report + plan, fixes Blockers->High->Medium->Low, re-runs validation; writes app_fix_reports/fix_<timestamp>.md.
grade4_closed_loops..claude/commands/build.md: Implements a plan top-to-bottom; report = bullet summary + git diff --stat (deliberately NO output template).
grade4_closed_loops.apps/orchestrator_3_stream/.claude/agent: opus review-agent template used by orch_plan_w_scouts_build_review (produces risk-tiered reports).

grade5_templates..claude/commands/plan.md: Grade-5 template: classifies task_type (chore|feature|refactor|fix|enhancement) + complexity (simple|medium|complex) and emits a conditional 'Plan Format' (Objective, Problem Statement, Solution Approach, Relevant Files, Implementation Phases, Step-by-Step Tasks, Testing Strategy, Acceptance Criteria, Validation Commands). Writes specs/<kebab>.md.
grade5_templates..claude/commands/plan_w_scouters.md: Same Plan Format template PLUS a scout swarm (3 scout-report-suggest + 5 scout-report-suggest-fast in parallel) that finds/validates relevant files before planning.
grade5_templates..claude/commands/quick-plan.md: model: claude-sonnet-4-5. Lightweight un-templated planner (bullet list, not a rigid format).

grade6_prompt_chains..claude/commands/build_in_parallel.md: model: sonnet. Decomposes a plan into per-file specs and launches multiple build-agent sub-agents in parallel.
grade6_prompt_chains..claude/commands/parallel_subagents.md: Generic 'launch COUNT parallel agents for PROMPT_REQUEST' fan-out primitive.
grade6_prompt_chains..claude/commands/plan_w_scouters.md: Scout-then-plan chain (see frame t1768's scout_then_plan.md on-screen equivalent).
grade6_prompt_chains..claude/commands/orch_scout_and_build.md: Two-phase orchestrator chain: scout (scout-report-suggest-fast) -> build (build-agent), polling with sleep + check_agent_status until a response->Stop hook.

grade7_experts..claude/commands/experts/adw/: ADW expert: expertise.yaml (407 lines; keys overview, workflow_types, composability, core_implementation, orchestrator_integration, websocket_events, frontend_integration, slash_commands, database_schema, execution_flow, best_practices, testing, key_file_locations, architecture_summary) + question.md (REUSE), plan.md (ACT), self-improve.md (LEARN, MAX_LINES 1000), plan_build_improve.md (full loop).
grade7_experts..claude/commands/experts/database/: Database expert (expertise.yaml 412 lines) — reduced 3-file expert (question, self-improve).
grade7_experts.apps/orchestrator_3_stream/backend/modul: The 'easter-egg' agent expert living INSIDE the orchestrator: a Haiku Claude Agent SDK agent with session persistence that learns from accepted/rejected completions and stores state in prompts/experts/orch_autocomplete/expertise.yaml.

class2_files.adws/adw_modules/adw_agent_sdk.py: 1655-line typed Pydantic wrapper for the Claude Agent SDK: ModelName enum (OPUS/OPUS_4_5=claude-opus-4-5-20251101, SONNET=claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929, HAIKU=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001), HooksConfig/HookMatcher, message models, TokenUsage/UsageAccumulator, BuiltInTool enum. Provides query_to_completion() and quick_prompt().
class2_files.adws/adw_workflows/adw_plan_build.py: 976 lines. 2-step ADW (TOTAL_STEPS=2): run_plan_step invokes '/plan <prompt>' (via the Skill tool), run_build_step invokes '/build <path>'. create_logging_hooks + create_message_handlers log every TextBlock/ThinkingBlock/ToolUseBlock and StepStart/StepEnd to the DB and broadcast to the swimlane UI.
class2_files.adws/adw_triggers/adw_manual_trigger.py: 355-line CLI trigger: creates an ADW DB record (like start_adw) and triggers the workflow via adw_scripts.py — 'test the complete flow without the orchestrator.' Usage: uv run adw_manual_trigger.py <name> <workflow_type> <prompt> <working_dir> [model].
class2_files.adws/adw_triggers/adw_scripts.py: 60 lines. run_adw_workflow_async(adw_id, workflow_type) spawns a detached background process: subprocess.Popen(['uv','run', adws/adw_workflows/adw_<type>.py, '--adw-id', adw_id], start_new_session=True). The workflow re-fetches prompt/working_dir from the DB by adw_id.
class2_files.adws/adw_modules/adw_websockets.py: Resilient WebSocket broadcaster (adw_created, adw_event, adw_step_change, adw_status) that fails silently if the server is down.
class2_files.adws/adw_modules/adw_summarizer.py: Claude-Haiku one-sentence event summaries for the swimlane UI.
class2_files.adws/adw_tests/adw_modules/adw_agent_sdk: Tests for the typed agent-SDK wrapper.

class3_files.apps/orchestrator_3_stream/backend/promp: 253-line orchestrator system prompt: 'You are the Orchestrator Agent - a meta-agent that manages other Agents.' Documents the 8 agent tools + start_adw/check_adw, holds {{SUBAGENT_MAP}} and {{AVAILABLE_ADW_TYPES}} injection points, ADW-vs-direct decision table, and 'You are the conductor of this multi-agent orchestra.'

current_practice_gaps.gap: The class/grade ladder is a teaching model, not a fixed spec — real repos consolidate rungs
current_practice_gaps.why: The lesson presents crisp per-grade 'example project structures' (separate bug.md/feature.md/chore.md at Grade 5; an adw_webhook.py at Class 2 Grade 1). The working orchestrator-agent-with-adws repo consolidates several of these: templates live inside plan.md's task_type switch, and the out-loop entry is the start_adw MCP tool + CLI trigger rather than a literal inbound webhook. Teach the ladder as a maturity model; show the repo as one real, consolidated instantiation.

current_practice_gaps.gap: 'start adw:' chat syntax is illustrative; the real trigger is an MCP tool call
current_practice_gaps.why: The repo README shows 'start adw: plan_build_review: ...' as a chat command, but there is no literal string parser in the code (grep returns zero hits). The orchestrator LLM emits a start_adw tool call that writes a DB record and spawns a detached uv-run process. Modern Claude Code practice is exactly this: agents act by calling typed tools/MCP servers, not by the host string-matching chat text.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Skills, headless mode, and the Agent SDK have matured since the recording
current_practice_gaps.why: The lesson's Grade-3 'skills' and Class-2 'core Agent SDK' map 1:1 to today's first-class Agent Skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter + progressive disclosure) and the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TypeScript) with headless flags, structured outputs, hooks, and session resume. The repo already uses these (meta-skill, adw_agent_sdk.py typed wrapper), so the concepts are current; specific APIs/flags move fast and should be re-verified at publish.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Model/UI drift and the ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL default
current_practice_gaps.why: The recording shows Nov-2025-era Claude Code UI and the claude-*-4-5 family (opus-4-5 default). Newer model families and TUI will differ. Dan's standing guidance applies: treat models/UI as period detail, tactics as current. The orchestrator's model is a one-line config change (config.ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL).

current_practice_gaps.gap: Observability/hooks and permissions are deliberately under-emphasized here
current_practice_gaps.why: Dan explicitly scopes the lesson to raw impact, not observability or security ('logging, not observability; it's just impact'). Production agentic layers now lean harder on hooks (pre/post tool-use gates), permission modes, sandboxed bash, and org/user/project settings layering. The repo ships a rich hooks/observability spine (send_event.py -> localhost:4000) but no permission allowlist in settings.json — a gap a production reader should close.

lab.summary: Locate your class/grade in the orchestrator-agent-with-adws repo, then drive the full stack: run an ADW from the CLI (Class 2), then from the orchestrator UI (Class 3), and read the evidence. Full gradable spec in lab-spec.md.
setup: Clone/open agentic-horizon/orchestrator-agent-with-adws; cp .env.sample .env and set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY + DATABASE_URL (NeonDB free tier works).
Map the layers out loud: point to the Class-1 files (.claude/), Class-2 files (adws/), and Class-3 files (apps/orchestrator_3_stream) before running anything.
reproduce_dan: Class 2 from the CLI: uv run adws/adw_triggers/adw_manual_trigger.py "lab-feature" "plan_build" "<a small feature for one app under apps/>" "$(pwd)" — confirm a specs/ plan is written and the app changes.

Read adws/adw_workflows/adw_plan_build.py and point to TOTAL_STEPS, run_plan_step ('/plan'), run_build_step ('/build'), and the logging hooks — this is deterministic code orchestrating non-deterministic agents.

Class 3 from the UI: start the orchestrator (./start_be.sh & ./start_fe.sh, open http://127.0.0.1:5175). In chat, ask the orchestrator to start a plan_build_review ADW for a markdown-preview feature; watch the ADWS swimlane view and the LOGS view.

Open .claude/commands/experts/adw/ and run the expert loop: /experts:adw:question "How does start_adw spawn a workflow?" (REUSE), then /experts:adw:self-improve true (LEARN) and confirm expertise.yaml stays <=1000 lines and valid YAML.
grade_yourself: Write down your OWN codebase's current class + grade and the single next element you would add, with a one-paragraph justification.
Prove Grade 6's rule: run /plan and /build individually, then as a chain — show you can isolate a failure to one step.
pass_criteria: You can point to a real file in the repo for every Class-1 grade 2-7, Class-2 grade 1-2, and Class-3 grade 1-3.
An ADW ran end to end from BOTH the CLI trigger and the orchestrator, with a specs/ plan and (for review/fix workflows) an app_review/ or app_fix_reports/ artifact produced.
You can state the exact tool the orchestrator calls to run an ADW (start_adw) and what it spawns (a detached uv-run adw_<type>.py --adw-id process).
You ran an agent-expert question + self-improve and can explain ACT/LEARN/REUSE and why expertise.yaml is a mental model, not a source of truth.
You can name your own codebase's class/grade and its next rung without notes.
